items.followUp: State the main conclusions drawn from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Conveys that most of the atom contains no matter.
rubric.description: Concludes that most of the atom is empty space.

rubric.why: Identifies where the atom’s positive charge is concentrated.
rubric.description: States that positive charge is concentrated in the nucleus.

rubric.why: Recognises the small size of the central region that deflected alpha particles.
rubric.description: States that the nucleus is very small compared with the atom.

rubric.why: Identifies the location of nearly all the atom’s mass.
rubric.description: States that most of the atom’s mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

rubric.why: Includes the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus in Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, showing that most of an atom is empty space.
A few alpha particles were deflected, showing that the atom’s positive charge is concentrated in a central nucleus.
The nucleus is very small compared with the size of the atom.
Almost all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus.

items.followUp: Define a molecule and explain the difference between homoatomic and heteroatomic molecules, with an example of each.

rubric.why: Captures the defining meaning of a molecule.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as the smallest particle that can exist independently and retain the substance’s chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the smallest particle and 1 mark for independent existence or retention of chemical properties.

rubric.why: Identifies molecules made from atoms of the same element and gives an example.
rubric.description: Explains homoatomic molecules and gives a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the description with an example.

rubric.why: Identifies molecules made from atoms of different elements and gives an example.
rubric.description: Explains heteroatomic molecules and gives a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the description with an example.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
Homoatomic molecules contain atoms of the same element, for example, H₂ or O₂.
Heteroatomic molecules contain atoms of different elements, for example, H₂O or CO₂.

items.followUp: Explain the dipole–dipole interaction between molecules of hydrogen bromide (HBr).

rubric.why: Recognises that HCl molecules are polar and have dipoles.
rubric.description: States that an HCl molecule is polar.

rubric.why: Identifies the partially positive end of HCl.
rubric.description: Identifies hydrogen as partially positive.

rubric.why: Identifies the partially negative end of HCl.
rubric.description: Identifies chlorine as partially negative.

rubric.why: Explains the attraction between opposite partial charges.
rubric.description: States that the opposite ends of dipoles attract.

rubric.why: Identifies the attraction as intermolecular.
rubric.description: States that the attraction is between neighbouring molecules.

modelAnswer: An HCl molecule is polar because chlorine attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen.
Thus, hydrogen has a partial positive charge (Hδ⁺) and chlorine has a partial negative charge (Clδ⁻).
The partially positive hydrogen end of one HCl molecule is attracted to the partially negative chlorine end of a neighbouring molecule.
This attraction between the opposite ends of neighbouring polar molecules is called dipole–dipole interaction.

items.followUp: Define molarity and explain how to prepare 500 mL of a 1 M sodium chloride solution.

rubric.why: States what molarity measures.
rubric.description: Defines molarity as the number of moles of solute per unit volume of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Gives the relationship used to calculate molarity.
rubric.description: Writes the formula for molarity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Calculates the mass of NaOH needed for one litre of a 1 M solution.
rubric.description: States that 40 g of NaOH is required for 1 L of 1 M solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct mass.

rubric.why: Describes dissolving the solute and preparing the required final volume.
rubric.description: Dissolves the NaOH and makes the solution up to one litre.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an appropriate preparation procedure.

modelAnswer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution.
M = number of moles of solute / volume of solution in dm³ (M = n/V).
Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹.
Weigh 40 g of NaOH and dissolve it in a small amount of distilled water.
Transfer the solution to a one-litre volumetric flask, add distilled water up to the mark, and mix well.
